batchName: Empire: The Fall of the West (AD 395-476) - Easy Batch 1
chapterName: Empire: The Fall of the West (AD 395-476)

questions.question: Why had huge numbers of Goths been living inside the Roman Empire since 376?
options: They had been hired as marines
They were invited to farm Gaul
questions.explanation: The Goths were refugees fleeing the Huns, nomadic horsemen from the Eurasian steppe. Corrupt officials exploited them, and they rebelled.
questions.sourceQuote: Since 376, huge numbers of Goths, a Germanic people fleeing the Huns, had been living inside the empire.

questions.question: Through which gate did the Goths enter Rome on 24 August 410?
questions.explanation: The Goths came in through the Salarian Gate. Some said traitors had opened it, others that hunger had.
questions.sourceQuote: On 24 August 410 the Goths entered Rome through the Salarian Gate.

questions.question: What was the title of the famous work by an English historian that began appearing in 1776?
options: Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
questions.explanation: Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire began appearing in 1776. Its author blamed barbarians, Christians and the Romans' own quarrels.
questions.sourceQuote: Edward Gibbon, an English historian whose Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire began appearing in 1776, blamed barbarians, Christians and the Romans' own quarrels.

questions.question: What term do many scholars now use for the long transformation in which Roman culture outlived Roman power?
questions.explanation: Many scholars speak of 'late antiquity' to stress continuity rather than sudden collapse. They also question the neat end date of 476.
questions.sourceQuote: Many scholars now speak of “late antiquity”, a long transformation in which Roman culture lived on after Roman power ended.

questions.question: Which great port did the Vandals capture in 439 and make their capital?
questions.explanation: The Vandals took Carthage, in modern Tunisia. They made it the capital of an independent kingdom with a powerful navy.
questions.sourceQuote: In 439 they captured Carthage (*Carthago*), the great port in modern Tunisia, and made it the capital of an independent kingdom with a powerful navy.

questions.question: Who forced Romulus Augustulus to give up the throne on 4 September 476?
questions.explanation: Odoacer, a Germanic officer, deposed the last western emperor. He led mercenaries who had rebelled when promised land was denied them.
questions.sourceQuote: On 4 September 476 Odoacer forced Romulus Augustulus to give up the throne.

questions.question: How did the great general Aetius die in 454?
options: He died of fever at sea
He was stabbed by the emperor himself
He was lynched by a Roman mob
questions.explanation: The western emperor killed Aetius with his own hands. Some historians think the emperor wanted to rule for himself rather than through a powerful manager.
questions.sourceQuote: In 454 the western emperor, Valentinian III, stabbed his great general Aetius to death with his own hands.

questions.question: How did Alaric bring Rome to the brink of starvation in late 408?
options: He blocked grain ships on the Tiber
He seized the port of Carthage
He burned the farms of Campania
questions.explanation: Alaric cut off the grain ships coming up the Tiber. Rations fell to a third, and corpses lay unburied in the streets.
questions.sourceQuote: In late 408 Alaric marched on it unopposed and blocked the grain ships coming up the Tiber.

questions.question: The sack of 410 was the first time in roughly how long that Rome had fallen to a foreign enemy?
questions.explanation: Rome had not fallen to a foreign enemy for almost 800 years. The Goths plundered the city for three days.
questions.sourceQuote: It was the first time in almost 800 years that Rome had fallen to a foreign enemy.

questions.question: What did the mocking nickname 'Augustulus' mean?
questions.explanation: Rivals mocked the boy emperor as 'little Augustus'. His real name, Romulus Augustus, echoed Rome's founder and its first emperor.
questions.sourceQuote: The boy was named Romulus Augustus, after Rome's founder and its first emperor, but rivals mocked him as Romulus Augustulus, “little Augustus”.
